passages.happening:
After the messages to the seven churches, John looks up and sees something new: “After this I looked and saw a door standing open in heaven” (verse 1). The voice he heard at the start of the book, the voice that spoke ‘like a trumpet’, calls to him: “Come up here, and I will show you what must happen after these things” (verse 1).

“At once I was in the Spirit, and I saw a throne standing in heaven, with someone seated on it” (verse 2). John does not describe the one seated there. He sees only colour and light: “The One seated there looked like jasper and carnelian, and a rainbow that gleamed like an emerald encircled the throne” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
For two chapters the book has stayed on earth, in seven cities of the Roman province of Asia, with churches that were poor, or comfortable, or under pressure. Now the scene moves from earth to heaven. And notice the order. Before John sees any seal broken, any trumpet blown or any beast rise, he sees a throne, and someone is sitting on it. Whatever the churches are about to face, the one who rules the world is seated. Everything that follows in the book flows out of this room. The Greek word for throne, thronos, comes fourteen times in these eleven verses, more than anywhere else in the New Testament.

That mattered in Asia. Its cities competed for the honour of building temples to the emperor. Pergamum had a temple to Rome and Augustus from 29 BC, Smyrna won the right to build one to Tiberius in AD 26, and Ephesus dedicated a temple to Domitian's family in his own time. The Roman writer Suetonius reports that Domitian liked to be addressed as lord and god. In this chapter only the One on the throne is called ‘our Lord and God’ (verse 11). For a small church in one of those cities, that was not a pious phrase. It was a claim about who really rules.

The voice that calls John up is the one he heard at the beginning, when he turned and saw the risen Christ among the lampstands (1:10-13). Christ is not named in this chapter, but he is the one who brings John into the throne room.

John keeps a careful reserve. He never says what God looks like. He speaks only of light like precious stones and a rainbow like an emerald, so bright that he can only compare it to other things. Ezekiel did the same when he saw the throne of God.
passages.ot:
The scene is drawn from the great throne visions of the prophets. Ezekiel saw “the likeness of a throne with the appearance of sapphire, and on the throne high above was a figure like that of a man” (Ezekiel 1:26), and around him “The appearance of the brilliant light all around Him was like that of a rainbow in a cloud on a rainy day” (Ezekiel 1:28). Notice how carefully Ezekiel speaks: a likeness, an appearance.

Isaiah, in the temple, saw the same: “I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted” (Isaiah 6:1). And Daniel saw thrones set in place, and “the Ancient of Days took His seat” (Daniel 7:9).
passages.hard:
‘Come up here, and I will show you what must happen after these things.’ How should the rest of the book be read?

From this chapter on, Christians have read Revelation in four broad ways, and the book page sets them out more fully. Preterists read most of the visions as fulfilled in the first centuries, in the Jewish war and the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, or in the persecutions of Rome, or both, while still expecting Christ's final return. Historicists read the visions as a map of the church's history from the apostles to the end. Futurists read chapters 4 to 22 as events still to come, in a final period before Christ returns. Idealists read the book as a picture of the conflict between God and evil that comes again in every age. Many recent commentators combine these: the book spoke directly to its first readers, it shows patterns that recur, and it looks toward a real end. These notes do not choose.

One form of futurism, dispensationalism, takes the call ‘Come up here’ as a picture of the church being taken from the earth before a time of trouble. Most other readers see it simply as John's own call into the vision. These notes do not choose here either.

What every way of reading agrees on is the point of this chapter. God reigns now, and the story that follows unfolds from his throne.
passages.asks: Ask what difference it would make to face your own pressures knowing that the throne is not empty. Ask who or what in your life claims the place of ‘lord’. And ask whether you are content, as John was, to see God's glory without needing to describe or control it.

passages.t: Twenty-four elders, and fire before the throne
passages.happening:
Around the throne John sees other thrones: “Surrounding the throne were twenty-four other thrones, and on these thrones sat twenty-four elders dressed in white, with golden crowns on their heads” (verse 4).

He sees and hears a storm: “From the throne came flashes of lightning, and rumblings, and peals of thunder” (verse 5). And he sees fire: “Before the throne burned seven torches of fire. These are the seven Spirits of God” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The scene moves outward in rings from the centre: first the One seated, then the rainbow, then the elders on their thrones, then the torches, then (in the next verses) the sea and the living creatures.

The twenty-four elders sit on thrones of their own. They share in God's rule. They wear white, like the faithful few in Sardis who were promised that they would walk with Christ in white (3:4), and they wear golden crowns, like the crown of life promised to the faithful in Smyrna (2:10). Who they are is discussed below.

The lightning and thunder recall the day God came down on Mount Sinai to meet his people. Here they come from the throne itself. This is the presence of the same holy God.

And the seven torches of fire are explained by the book itself: ‘These are the seven Spirits of God.’ The phrase was used in the greeting at the start of the book (1:4). Seven is the number of completeness in Revelation, and many readers take the seven Spirits as the Holy Spirit in his fullness, before the throne.
passages.ot:
The thunder and lightning are Sinai's: “On the third day, when morning came, there was thunder and lightning. A thick cloud was upon the mountain, and a very loud blast of the ram’s horn went out, so that all the people in the camp trembled” (Exodus 19:16).

Daniel too saw more than one throne: “As I continued to watch, thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took His seat” (Daniel 7:9).

The seven lamps recall Zechariah's vision of a lampstand: “I see a solid gold lampstand,” he says, “with a bowl at the top and seven lamps on it” (Zechariah 4:2).
passages.hard:
Who are the twenty-four elders? And what are ‘the seven Spirits of God’?

The elders are read in several ways. Many take them as the whole people of God, the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles together, since the new Jerusalem in chapter 21 bears both sets of names on its gates and foundations (21:12-14). Others see them as heavenly counterparts to the twenty-four divisions of priests who served in the temple (1 Chronicles 24). Others take them as a council of angels around God's throne. These notes do not choose.

The seven Spirits are read as they were at 1:4. Many take them as the Holy Spirit in his fullness, since seven is the number of completeness and Zechariah 4 pictures a lampstand with seven lamps. Some read them as seven chief angels. These notes do not choose.

Either way, the picture is the same: before anything happens on earth, heaven is full of worship and order around the one God.
passages.asks: Ask what it means that those around God's throne wear crowns and still bow. Ask whether the God you pray to is as holy as the God of Sinai and of this room. And ask what it would mean to you that God's Spirit burns before his throne in fullness.

passages.happening:
“And before the throne was something like a sea of glass, as clear as crystal” (verse 6). Around the throne John sees four living creatures, “covered with eyes in front and back” (verse 6).

“The first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third had a face like a man, and the fourth was like an eagle in flight” (verse 7). Each has six wings and is covered with eyes. And John hears their song, which never stops: “Day and night they never stop saying: ‘Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!’” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world the sea was a picture of chaos and danger, the deep that no one could tame. Here, before God, it lies flat and still, clear as glass. Some readers also hear an echo of the great bronze basin in Solomon's temple, which was called ‘the Sea’.

The four ‘living creatures’ are given an ordinary Greek word, zōon, which simply means a living being or an animal. Many interpreters see the four as standing for the whole of living creation: the wild beast, the farm animal, the human being and the bird. If so, the whole created world is here leading the worship of its maker. Their eyes are everywhere. They see.

Their song is the heart of the chapter. ‘Holy, Holy, Holy’ names God as utterly other and utterly pure. Heaven's worship begins not with requests but with the plain recognition of who God is.

‘The Lord God Almighty’ translates a Greek word, pantokratōr, the ruler of all. In the Greek Old Testament it often stands for the title ‘LORD of Hosts’. Apart from one verse in Paul (2 Corinthians 6:18), the New Testament uses it only in Revelation, where it sets God's rule above every power that claims to rule.

And God is the one ‘who was and is and is to come’. He was before every empire, he is now, and he is the one who comes at the end.
passages.ot:
The living creatures come from Ezekiel's vision, where each had four faces: “The form of their faces was that of a man, and each of the four had the face of a lion on the right side, the face of an ox on the left side, and also the face of an eagle” (Ezekiel 1:10). Ezekiel also saw that the rims of the wheels beside them “were full of eyes all around” (Ezekiel 1:18).

The six wings and the threefold cry come from Isaiah's seraphim: “Above Him stood seraphim, each having six wings” (Isaiah 6:2), “And they were calling out to one another: ‘Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory’” (Isaiah 6:3).

And the name ‘who was and is and is to come’ echoes God's own name given to Moses at the burning bush: “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14).
passages.hard:
Is heaven really like this, with creatures covered in eyes and a sea of glass?

Revelation is a book of pictures, and the book page explains how it works. Its symbols are meant to be understood, and most of them come from the Old Testament. John takes Ezekiel's creatures and Isaiah's seraphim and puts them together. He keeps their strangeness, because God is not like anything in this world. And he refuses to describe God himself at all.

So these notes do not try to draw a map of heaven from this chapter. The picture tells the truth in its own way: God is holy, creation was made to worship him, and nothing is hidden from his sight.
passages.asks: Ask when you last praised God simply for who he is, without asking for anything. Ask what in your life feels like a stormy sea, and what it means that before God the sea lies still. And ask whether you think of the whole created world, animals included, as joining in the praise of God.

passages.happening:
Whenever the living creatures give glory, honour and thanks to the One on the throne, John sees the elders join in: “the twenty-four elders fall down before the One seated on the throne, and they worship Him who lives forever and ever” (verse 10).

“They cast their crowns before the throne, saying: ‘Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things; by Your will they exist and came to be’” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
Two songs close the chapter. The living creatures praise God for who he is: holy, almighty, eternal. The elders praise him for what he has done: he created all things, and by his will they exist.

‘Worthy’ translates the Greek word axios. It was used in public acclamations of rulers. Crowds shouted it to kings and emperors. Here it is said of God as Creator. In the next chapter the same word will be sung to the Lamb.

And the elders cast their crowns before the throne. Laying a crown before a greater king was a known gesture in the Roman world. The historian Tacitus records that in AD 63 the Parthian prince Tiridates laid his royal diadem before a statue of Nero. The elders wear crowns, but they do not keep them. Every honour they have, they hand back to the one who made them.

Creation is the ground of their praise. Because God made all things, he has the right to rule them and to judge them, and no emperor or power can claim the worship that belongs to him.

The chapter ends with the throne room full of praise. Chapter 5 will bring a sealed scroll and a slain Lamb into this same room, and the Lamb will receive the same worship in the same words. That is one of the clearest places in the New Testament where Jesus is worshipped as God is worshipped. The church would later confess in the Nicene Creed that the Son is ‘true God from true God’, and Revelation is one of the places that faith rests on.
passages.ot:
The elders' song is Israel's own faith in God the Creator. The Levites prayed, “You alone are the LORD. You created the heavens, the highest heavens with all their host, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them. You give life to all things, and the host of heaven worships You” (Nehemiah 9:6).

The psalm says the same: “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth” (Psalm 33:6). And it calls the heavenly beings to do what the elders do here: “Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength” (Psalm 29:1).
passages.asks: Ask what crowns you are holding on to: achievements, titles, honours. Ask what it would mean to lay them down before God. And ask whether you praise God more easily for who he is, or for what he has made, and why.
